title: The councils
hook: bishops met at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) to settle who Jesus is
tomorrow: the ancient churches of the east

segments.voice: Yesterday, one church, then many: a thousand years of broadly one church, with arguments, and then the splits. Your line was one body many parts. Which church not your own did you hold in mind? Day two hundred eighty-three.

Picture the year 325, in a lakeside town called Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. Around three hundred bishops arrive, some on imperial horses, paid for by the emperor Constantine. A few of them carry scars. Only a dozen years earlier, Christians were being arrested and tortured, and some of these old men still limp from it. Now the emperor has called them together, because the church is arguing so loudly it can be heard in the marketplace. A priest from Alexandria named Arius has been teaching that the Son of God was created, the first and greatest of all creatures, but a creature. People are setting his ideas to catchy songs. Others are furious. So the bishops sit down in one room to answer a question that sounds simple: who is Jesus? Today's word is the room.
screen: `NICAEA, THE YEAR 325.` → `BISHOPS WITH SCARS.` → `WHO IS JESUS?`

segments.voice: A council is a gathering of church leaders to settle something together. The Greek word is synodos, a way taken together, the root of our word synod. The idea goes back to the Bible itself: in Acts 15 the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem to argue about whether new believers must keep the Jewish law, and they send out a letter that says, it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us. At Nicaea, the bishops rejected Arius. They wrote a statement saying the Son is of one being with the Father, one Greek word, homoousios. Fifty-six years later, a second council, at Constantinople, expanded it into the creed most churches still say, known as the Nicene Creed. In the old English of the Book of Common Prayer it says the Son is "God of God, Light of Light, Very God of very God, Begotten, not made." Then in 451, at Chalcedon, another council asked the next question: if Jesus is truly God, is he truly human too? Their answer was yes, one person, two natures, not mixed and not split. We'll come back to that one. Two things are worth knowing. First, the councils didn't invent faith in Jesus; they tried to put into words what churches were already praying and singing, and they argued fiercely doing it, with politics mixed in. Second, not everyone accepted every council. Chalcedon, especially, led to a lasting split, which is tomorrow's story. And notice how the council's creed began: not I believe, but we believe.
screen: `SYNODOS: A WAY TAKEN TOGETHER.` · `NICAEA: OF ONE BEING WITH THE FATHER.` · `CHALCEDON: TRULY GOD, TRULY HUMAN.` · `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.` · then, large: `BEGOTTEN, NOT MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the Nicene Creed once. You can find it in almost any prayer book, or online. Read it slowly, the way you'd read a letter from someone who had suffered to write it. Notice which line stops you: the one you love, or the one you don't understand. If you pray, you can say it aloud. If you don't, just read it as a very old answer to a very old question. Then settle, breathe, and let that one line sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Council. Church leaders gathered to settle a question together. From Jerusalem to Nicaea to Chalcedon.
Your line: we believe. Today, notice one thing you believe that you didn't work out alone, something you were handed by people who came before. Day two hundred eighty-three.

screen: `DAY 283 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ANCIENT CHURCHES OF THE EAST.`

howItsDone: Many churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and others, say the Nicene Creed together at the main Sunday service, usually standing, after the readings and sermon.

original.note: Greek: syn, together, and hodos, a way or road. A meeting, a council: the root of synod.

trapdoor: what you thought: a council is a committee that votes on rules.
what it means: church leaders gathered to put their shared faith into words, especially about who Jesus is.
what a scholar hears: synodos, a way taken together. Nicaea's one key word, homoousios, isn't in the Bible, and that was part of the fight.

sources.ref: Creed of Nicaea (325); Definition of Chalcedon (451)

notes: Number of bishops at Nicaea: tradition says 318; modern estimates run about 250–300. Script says 'around three hundred'.
Scarred bishops (e.g. Paphnutius) is a tradition reported by later historians; script says 'a few of them carry scars'. Confirm tone.
Arius's ideas set to songs (the Thalia) is reported by his opponents; confirm.
Council of Constantinople (381) expanded the creed; the text used today is often called the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. Script says 'fifty-six years later'.
The original creed of 325 began 'We believe' (pisteuomen); many liturgical English versions say 'I believe'. Confirm the closing point.
Chalcedon's formula is paraphrased; day 301 returns to it.
Acts 15:28 is not the opening of the Jerusalem letter (it opens at 15:23); the teach now says the letter 'says' this rather than 'begins' with it.
